newsitem.title: USA: Penney deal shows retailers diversifying.
newsitem.headline: Penney deal shows retailers diversifying.

text.p: J.C. Penney Co's agreement to buy Eckerd Corp shows retailers again are diversifying to grow, but the risks are lower now than during buying binges of the past, experts said Monday.

Penney, the fifth-largest U.S. retailer, announced Sunday it would acquire Eckerd in a deal valued at about $3.2 billion. When the transaction is completed, Penney's Thrift drugstore chain would be the third largest in the business.
Dallas-based Penney has swallowed two other drug chains and a big piece of a third during the past 18 months.
Penney's moves come as expansion in the saturated department-store sector has slowed to a trickle, forcing traditional retailers to diversify to grow.

"They have some real tough competitive issues in their core business," said Michael Exstein of PaineWebber. "The issue for them is how do they harness their financial resources to offset an intense business (environment)."
While Penney has been in the drugstore business for a quarter century, the company only recently turned to that sector to boost stagnant revenues and energize profits.

Under the deal, Penney would offer $35 a share for about half of Eckerd's shares. In a second stage, Eckerd holders would receive 0.6604 Penney share for each Eckerd share, and Penney would assume $760 million in Eckerd debt, putting the value of the deal at about $3.2 billion.
Penney's shares fell $2 to $51 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.

The deal would dilute Penney's earnings by about $0.20 a share in 1997 and add to earnings the next year. It also would leverage Penney's balance sheet, raising its debt to capital ratio to an estimated 60 percent from 43 percent, S&P said.
